Substandard stopping sight distance for the bridge and approach roadways will be eliminated.  The design speed for the bridge and approach roadways is 60 MPH (100 KMPH). agency_project_description: The existing 17th Avenue and 27th Avenue Pedestrian Bridges over Belt-Parkway were constructed under the Robert Moses era Master Plan for NYC.  Because the existing 17th Avenue and 27th Avenue Pedestrian Bridges, sloping over the Belt Parkway Highway, achieve their maximum height only at the apex of their spans, they have been repeatedly impacted by errant trucks coming from the Verrazano Narrows Bridge and the Brooklyn Queens Expressway, thereby causing significant damage to the existing superstructures.  The existing bridges do not provide ADA compliant access. Due to these circumstances the existing bridges cannot be modified to meet the project goals. The total replacement will include:  precast steel grid bridge deck system, replacement of the substructure (abutments) and arch superstructure with the intention to reflect the historic design, new minimum clear width of 12’- 0” and a vertical clearance of 15’- 6”, installation of new railings, fencing, lighting, traffic signals, drainage and accessible ramps/stairway. The structure will also meet the latest Seismic code requirements and ADA compliance.

This project will completely replace the roadway bridge structure which was last rehabilitated in 1982 and originally constructed in 1906 (subway structure added in 1917).  Replacement of the deteriorated subway structural elements will also be a part of this project.  In addition to the bridge work, the project will also incorporate the following pedestrian improvements which are consistent with NYC’s Vision Zero and OneNYC objectives:• Curb extensions will be added at street corners to reduce the pedestrian crossing distance at both 151st and 153rd Streets and sidewalk limits will be generally be expanding throughout the project limits.• The raised concrete median in the center of Grand Concourse will be widened which will reduce pedestrian crossing distance while also creating space for a future bicycle lane.• ADA compliant pedestrian ramps will be installed at all pedestrian crossing within the project limits along with high-visibility crosswalks.• The Grand Concourse northbound 153rd Street MTA bus stop concrete island will be expanded while maintaining existing bush and tree plantings.• Street lighting was re-analyzed and the proposed design will improve on the existing lighting conditions.  All new street lights will have LED luminaires installed as well as any existing street lights that are remaining.  The proposed street lights will use historic Type M poles and luminaires to match the aesthetics of the Grand Concourse Historic District.

agency_project_description: This capital project will address the East 169th Street step street’s substandard condition through full reconstruction of the project area. Consistent with other step street projects, the design consultant for this project shall provide several design alternatives for the project limits, with attention paid to maximizing accessibility, public space, functionality, and streetscape amenities (street trees, seating, etc.) within the right of way. DOT acknowledges that many of these priorities are competing for limited space within this constrained project site, and that the different alternatives will prioritize these competing interests differently.DOT’s preliminary accessibility analysis suggests that a combination of ADA accessible ramps and staircases are feasible within the project limits (see this document’s conceptual design attachment for a proof of concept). This scale diagram establishes that there is sufficient space for a ramp structure within the project limits. DDC shall direct the design consultant to explore various ramp and stair configurations during preliminary design and identify any technical challenges associated with their construction. If, after reviewing the design alternatives, it is determined only stairway accessibility can be provided, any technical infeasibility or other constraint that limits building to full ADA requirements must be fully documented and added to the project file. The documentation must, at a minimum, clearly lay out the issue, describe the efforts taken to rectify the issue, and explain why the final design was chosen to be selected.

agency_project_description: The Bergen Building, located in the Tremont area of the Bronx and fronting the main pedestrian entrance of the William Gladwin Park, is composed of two separate adjacent buildings built in 1912 and 1916. In the mid-1930s, the City purchased both buildings and joined them. The building currently is leased to several not-for-profits and city agencies. The Department of Citywide Administrative Services manages and maintains the building. In 2014, DCAS, working with Mayor DeBlasio’s office identified the building as a candidate for significant energy improvements in line with the goals of the OneNYC. The City engaged Studio Gang to conduct a Pre-Schematic Design Report in anticipation of these upgrades, which detailed three levels of proposed energy improvements, bronze, silver and gold, with estimates and ambitious energy performance scope proposals.As part of this analysis, and others, major code compliance issues have been identified on the interior of the building, including travel distances, exit separation, restroom configuration and fixture counts, and accessibility issues. The building’s façade has been deficient for decades and has been determined scientifically to be a mold habitat. The fire alarm system is obsolete. Much of the wiring is original, and there is not enough electric capacity for a new HVAC system. The building requires a new sprinkler standpipe. Previous efforts to initiate Studio Gang’s proposals were underfunded. In the meantime, the building continued to degrade, and most grievously, the envelope lack of watertightness continues to take its toll.Accordingly, priority has been given to the stabilization of the envelope, as the current project initiation request makes clear. There is a budget of almost $40M to make the building watertight by replacing the roof, rehabilitating the masonry, replacing the windows, and installing a rain screen on the most porous surfaces. Critically, DCAS/Real Estate has identified required swing space to enable this work while the building remains open; new scope for this swing is included. There is cross-bracing in the rear yard which requires rehabilitation to address the façade.

agency_project_description: The proposed project involves the reconstruction and replacement of a short length of an existing sewer and an outfall that discharges into Bowery Bay (see Figures C-4a and C-4b); this sewer and outfall reconstruction is proposed to address what is currently a partially collapsed outfall. Replacement would restore the outfall’s necessary functions and avoid a potential full collapse and failure. Specifically, the proposed project includes the following: Installation of a new a 14-foot 7-inch-wide by 8-foot-high combined sewer outfall (referenced as the Bowery Bay [BB]-005 outfall) which discharges into Bowery Bay, thereby replacing the currently collapsed outfall. The proposed outfall would be reconstructed at the same location as the existing outfall and within an existing sewer easement across land that is owned by the City of New York and under the jurisdiction of the Department of Small Business Services. The proposed sewer and outfall design calls for a reinforced concrete structure supported on a concrete cradle with a flap gate at the outlet to control any inflow of tidal water from the bay. Additionally, boulders are proposed to be installed to stabilize the bottom of the bay to minimize the potential for scour and resuspension of sediments into the water column that may otherwise occur when there is flow from the outfall. Reconstruction of a 60-foot-long by 14-foot-7-inch wide and 8-foot-high combined sewer that flows into and connects with the proposed outfall.
